# The History of the Roman Empire

The Roman Empire stands as one of the most influential civilizations in human history, shaping law, governance, architecture, and culture across millennia. Its story spans over a thousand years, from the legendary founding of Rome in 753 BCE to the fall of the Western Empire in 476 CE.

## The Kingdom and Republic

According to tradition, Rome was founded by Romulus and Remus, twin brothers raised by a she-wolf. The early Roman Kingdom lasted until 509 BCE, when the last king, Tarquin the Proud, was expelled, establishing the Roman Republic. This new system introduced elected magistrates and the Senate, creating a government that balanced power among aristocrats.

During the Republic, Rome expanded steadily through conquest. The Punic Wars (264-146 BCE) against Carthage proved transformative. After three devastating conflicts, Rome destroyed Carthage and gained control of the western Mediterranean. Concurrently, conquests in Greece, Asia Minor, and the Near East brought eastern territories under Roman influence.

The late Republic saw growing instability. Military commanders like Marius, Sulla, and later Julius Caesar amassed personal loyalty from their legions, undermining senatorial authority. Caesar's assassination in 44 BCE sparked civil wars that ultimately destroyed the Republic.

## The Principate and Empire

Augustus, Caesar's adopted son, emerged victorious from the civil wars. In 27 BCE, he cleverly maintained republican forms while accumulating imperial power, inaugurating the Pax Romana—a roughly 200-year period of relative peace and prosperity.
